Info

Where the game comes from and how the two browser editions work.

The original game

David L. Clark created Sopwith for BMB Compuscience in 1984, followed by Sopwith II in 1985. Its released C source became the basis for SDL Sopwith, maintained by Simon Howard and contributors.

This project uses SDL Sopwith 2.9.0. Its source and original graphics remain unchanged in third_party/sdl-sopwith/. Browser integration and Rainbow-specific rules live separately under web/. The DOS game is a reference; exact equivalence with its physics and AI has not been established. Original authorship and license notices accompany both editions.

Two editions

Sopwith II retains the native CGA renderer and PC speaker sound. Rainbow Patrol adds painted scenery, detailed sprites, arcade menus and a wood, leather and brass cockpit around the same C game foundation.

Rainbow has three missions: a sunny coast, snowy valleys and a mountainous, storm-damaged city. Each mission has a different terrain profile while preserving safe airfield heights. Easy disables ground return fire; Normal enables it from mission one. Enemy aircraft are an independent optional extra. Completing mission three ends the campaign at the medal ceremony and Badge of Honor score board.

The native simulation runs at ten steps per second. A JavaScript display timeline interpolates positions, camera motion, aircraft angles, speed and throttle between steps. Canvas 2D draws a 1920 × 1488 framebuffer: a 640 × 400 logical flight area plus a 96-pixel cockpit, rendered at three times the resolution. Local checks target smooth 60 FPS rendering; results depend on the device. This implementation uses neither Rust, WebGL nor Three.js.

C, SDL and WebAssembly

TechnologyRole
CGame logic, flight, AI, collisions, weapons and the classic renderer.
SDL2Video, keyboard and audio interfaces adapted to browser facilities.
Emscripten 4.0.10Compiles the C game and SDL2 into WebAssembly and its JavaScript loader.
WebAssemblyThe executable game module, sopwith.wasm, runs locally in the browser.
JavaScript, HTML and CSSLoading, display interpolation, menus, sample audio and on-screen controls.
IndexedDB / localStorageNative settings, browser preferences and local high scores.
GitHub Actions / PagesAutomated builds, checks and static hosting.

Asyncify lets the original blocking game loop yield to the browser. Pause freezes game time. The published game runs a source-built WASM module; it does not emulate the original EXE.

The classic image is 320 × 200 with a cyan/magenta/white CGA palette or the alternate green/red/yellow palette.

Flight and instruments

Rainbow has sixteen throttle positions and gradual acceleration, with substantially more speed at full throttle. The cockpit shows throttle percentage, airspeed in MPH, altitude in feet above ground, fuel, ammunition and remaining bomb icons. The instrument conversion is an arcade scale: 18 km/h per native speed unit and 10 metres per native vertical pixel. The airspeed face marks nominal level-flight stall speed at 52 MPH and takeoff at 60 MPH; climbing or damage can cause an earlier stall. The altimeter has a traditional 0–9 dial, hundreds/thousands hands and an FT AGL counter. Ornamental hands and glass reflections are separate sprite layers. Winter adds light frost; the storm mission uses warm cockpit lamps, lightning and delayed synthesized thunder.

Hold B to show the bomb guide, then release to drop one bomb. A quick tap also drops one. Five bombs fit the magazine; returning home replenishes supplies. The guide predicts terrain impact and does not account for intervening buildings. Bullets and native collision masks remain part of the C simulation. Large architecture takes two bombs, one bomb plus twelve bullets, or twenty-four bullets. Each building has separate intact, one-bomb damaged and destroyed artwork; the damaged state starts at half health.

Parachutists descend, land and walk to their own airfield. Shooting either side while airborne costs 1000 points; shooting a friendly on the ground costs 500, while a hostile on foot awards 100. Friendly ground crew can pass departing aircraft safely. Defenses are separate AA emplacements and tanks rather than invisible building guns.

Every aircraft gets a 2.5-second READY badge. First-life inactivity shows takeoff keys after five seconds. Mission completion uses a dedicated rear-view aircraft animation before the next mission. Autopilot navigation reads the current terrain and adds clearance assistance around generated slopes and buildings. Ground textures follow the mutable terrain; craters use the current mission surface and cannot raise lowered hills.

Controls and development trainer

Open Controls in either game. In flight, X/Z adjust throttle, comma/slash pitch, period rolls, Space fires, B releases a bomb and H returns home. Arrows also work. P or Escape pauses; S toggles sound. Native classic menus retain their original letter shortcuts.

During development, Rainbow’s trainer starts on. Switch it off in Settings for a ranked run. It provides unlimited lives, fuel, bombs and ammunition; aircraft can still crash. Trainer flights never enter the high score list. With trainer enabled, number keys 1–9 jump to a level and E clears the mission and starts its departure sequence. Levels beyond three are development previews that cycle the three environments.

The console commands remain available in both editions:

trainer()
trainer(false)

The temporary default and test controls will be removed before the final release. Sound always starts off.

High scores

Scores currently persist in this browser. The repository includes a separate shared leaderboard service, but no public endpoint is configured. Aircraft-enabled and ground-only games have separate boards, as do Easy and Normal.

Enter three letters or digits directly on your ranked row. Up/down changes a character, left/right moves the cursor and Enter saves. Up to ten rows remain visible around your rank during entry; saving ends on the top-ten list. A completed campaign uses the medal-ceremony background. Trainer scores are excluded.

AI wingman

Mission Setup offers an optional friendly escort, marked 2. It departs shortly after you, follows behind and above, and engages nearby hostile aircraft. It returns with you or when supplies are low. Enemy fire and terrain can still bring it down; friendly formation contacts are protected. It uses the existing painted aircraft, wreck and pilot assets. This first version does not bomb ground targets. Two-human-player control is future work.

Wingman runs have separate local scoreboards, keeping assisted results out of solo/shared lists. Mission Setup also explains Rookie/Ace rules and shows a paper briefing chart built from the native terrain and target roster.

Artwork and audio credits

New artwork was created for this project using built-in OpenAI imagegen. Settings has its own ground-crew workshop with a left-hand slate. Original PNGs, prompts and hashes are documented in ARTWORK.md and the corresponding source archive. Amiga games, Rainbow Islands, RETRY and Wings informed the visual direction; their game assets are not distributed here.

Kenney’s Sci-fi Sounds and Impact Sounds are CC0. Additional CC0 recordings include Joseph SARDIN’s Moo 0845 and bird sound, spurioustransients’ cow sound, Graciano Choc / gchoc’s fanfare, kirbydx’s sad trombone and EZduzziteh’s Hurt Sound Effects. The repeatedly triggered target fanfare is disabled.

The short startup and quiet, speed-sensitive engine loop derive from Torsten Nilsson’s radial engine recording, CC BY 4.0, shortened, converted to mono and faded. Jeuwre’s De-Himmel.ogg is CC BY-SA 4.0; the trimmed, filtered and normalized adaptation retains that license.

Title and debrief music: Spring Spring, War Theme, version 2, CC0, converted to 22,050 Hz stereo. Music plays only after sound is enabled. Rainbow’s five-voice Web Audio mixer loads samples lazily; mute and hidden tabs stop playback. The cockpit engine changes pitch with throttle, speed and descent. Takeoff requires about 60 MPH; slow climbs can stall, with recovery by lowering the nose and adding power. Large architecture takes two bombs, a bomb plus twelve bullets, or twenty-four bullets.

The falling-aircraft sound was created and supplied by the project owner: Falling aircraft — generated with elevenlabs.io. Its four-second adaptation plays once per fall under separate ElevenLabs terms; it is not labeled CC0 or GPL audio. Rainbow’s menus and instruments use original Patrol Chalk and Patrol Engraved fonts, traced from this project’s illustrated glyph atlases and distributed with the GPL v2+ game. High scores use bronze nameplates on timber with engraved initials and scores; the classroom retains its shared chalkboard with navigation outside the writing surface. Their PNGs, conversion script and exact hashes accompany the source. Earlier Patrick Hand and Press Start 2P assets retain their OFL 1.1 notices.
